name: Cold-pressed raw milk bath

card.summary: A milk bath is soaking in milk, in the style attributed to Cleopatra, to soften skin and lift dead cells for a smoother, brighter look.
card.note: Beauty claims come mostly from history and folklore.

quick.overview:
A milk bath is a bath taken in milk instead of, or added to, water, often scented with honey, rose or essential oils. Fans say it leaves skin soft and bright.

The appearance logic is that milk's lactic acid, an alpha hydroxy acid, loosens the proteins holding dead skin cells together, giving a smoother surface. The practice is linked to Cleopatra and Poppaea in legend, and to queens such as Elizabeth I.
quick.how: People add milk or milk powder, sometimes with flower petals or oils, to a warm bath and soak. Raw or cold-pressed milk versions are favoured by some for being unprocessed.
quick.risks: Milk baths are generally a topical soak; people with milk allergy or sensitive skin may react, and milk left in warm water can sour.

lead: A milk bath is a bath in milk, often scented with honey, rose, daisies or essential oils, used for a soft, smooth complexion.[1]

The practice is tied in legend to Cleopatra bathing in donkey milk, though this is unconfirmed. Historian Adrian Goldsworthy believes Empress Poppaea set the fashion about 80 years after Cleopatra's death.[1] Queens Catherine Parr and Elizabeth I reportedly bathed in milk to look younger and paler.[1]

The article explains the claimed action through lactic acid, an alpha hydroxy acid that dissolves proteins holding dead skin cells together.[1] Commercial products include a Chinese patent for a milk bath salt and a donkey milk cosmetic claimed to moisturise and whiten.[2][3]

chain: Lactic acid loosens dead skin cells
angle.text: Soakers use milk baths for softer, brighter-looking skin, relying on the mild exfoliating effect of lactic acid.

paras: Cleopatra became associated with milk baths mainly through Claudette Colbert's 1930s film portrayals of her and Poppaea. Anna Held was also reported to bathe in milk. Buttermilk baths were historically a grooming method for show animals.[1]

Patents describe a milk bath salt mixing milk with salt and fragrance for beauty and health care, and a donkey milk cosmetic with over 30 percent donkey milk positioned as moisturiser and whitening agent.[2][3]
